title: How Design Ops built an AI teammate with no engineering lift
summary: No engineers. No code. Design Ops built an AI teammate that answers questions in seconds, not hours — and discovered the real challenge was the documentation, not the technology.
body_markdown:
Our Design Ops team supports more than 600 designers across Atlassian. And like most operations teams, we were seeing the same pattern over and over again: important questions landing in Slack, manual triage happening in the background, and too much useful knowledge trapped in docs that people either couldn’t find or didn’t have time to read.


We built DOT, the Design Org Teammate, to change that. DOT is an AI agent that helps answer common tooling questions in our help channel, using the knowledge our team had already built in Confluence and a no-code configuration in Rovo Studio.


This is the story of the problem we were trying to solve, how we built DOT as a non-technical team, what we learned along the way, and what changed once it went live.


# The problem: too much knowledge, not enough access


Design Ops sits in the middle of a lot of day-to-day questions: How do I get access to a tool? What’s the approved path for trying something new? Why did my credits run out? Where does this request belong? Which page has the latest guidance?


For a while, the operating model was simple but fragile. A designer would ask in the help channel, someone on Design Ops would pick it up, find the right answer, and reply. That worked — until scale caught up with it.


**We were dealing with a few overlapping problems:**


- Knowledge existed, but it wasn’t always easy to retrieve in the moment.
- Answers depended on who was online, what they knew, and how quickly they saw the request.
- The same questions kept coming back, but still required manual handling each time.
- People preferred asking in chat to searching through documentation.


The result was a support model that relied too heavily on human memory and human availability. It also meant some questions were answered slowly, inconsistently, or not at all.


We didn’t need a generic chatbot. We needed a reliable teammate that could meet people where they already worked, answer the questions that were genuinely repeatable, and hand off cleanly when judgment or follow-up was needed.


# How we built DOT


The unusual part of this project is that we built it from inside Design Ops. We’re not an engineering team. We didn’t spin up a custom service or write a production codebase. We used the tools already available to us and treated the build like an operations problem: define the use case, improve the source material, configure carefully, test honestly, and launch narrowly.


## Built in Rovo Studio


DOT was built in[Rovo Studio](https://www.atlassian.com/software/rovo/studio) , Atlassian’s no-code environment for creating AI agents. That mattered because it removed the biggest blocker many non-technical teams face: dependency on engineering capacity before they can even learn what’s possible.


That gave us room to experiment quickly, make changes directly, and keep the work close to the people who understood the support problem best.


## A simple configuration model


Under the hood, DOT followed a simple pattern:


1. **Trigger:** the kind of question DOT should respond to
2. **Instructions:** how DOT should behave, what it should and shouldn’t do, and when to hand off
3. **Knowledge sources:** the Confluence content DOT should rely on to answer accurately


We started small, focusing on tooling questions in the help channel. That gave us a clear scope and a manageable test bed. Instead of trying to support every kind of request from day one, we concentrated on the categories that were both common and documentable: tool access, tooling issues, and related process questions.


## Designing a teammate, not a bot


One of the most important choices we made was to define DOT’s voice intentionally. We didn’t want it to sound like a support script or an FAQ generator. We wanted it to feel like a capable teammate: direct, warm, clear about its limits, and useful in the moment.


That meant writing much more explicit guidance than “be friendly” or “be helpful.” We set expectations for tone, structure, scope, and escalation. DOT was instructed to answer first, explain second; use plain English; avoid guesswork; and be honest when a question needed a human.


That work paid off. The more clearly we described who DOT was and how it should behave, the more reliable its responses became.


# The hardest part wasn’t the agent. It was the knowledge


The biggest lesson from the project was simple: an AI agent will expose the quality of your documentation very quickly.


At first, we assumed the main challenge would be configuring the agent well. In practice, the harder challenge was making sure the source content was strong enough to support it. Some pages were too vague. Some buried the real answer halfway down. Some assumed a human reader would fill in the gaps. That works better for people than it does for machines.


We ended up adopting a new mindset: **every page is a promise** .


If a page was going to sit inside DOT’s knowledge sources, it had to be accurate, current, specific, and structured in a way that made retrieval reliable.


**That led to a lot of behind-the-scenes work:**


- rewriting pages to make key actions obvious
- removing ambiguous language
- bringing buried process steps to the top
- filling documentation gaps where no good answer existed yet
- thinking about content ownership and maintenance, not just publication


That work improved DOT, but it also improved the human self-serve experience. Better knowledge for the agent turned out to mean better knowledge for the team.


### Pro Tip


If you’re building an AI teammate, start with the content. A well-scoped agent on strong documentation will outperform a more sophisticated setup grounded in vague, stale, or scattered knowledge.


# What we got wrong, and what we changed


We learned quickly that building a useful agent is less about getting everything right the first time and more about tightening the loop between configuration, evaluation, and content improvement.


#### 1. We overestimated our documentation coverage


Early evaluations showed DOT could handle straightforward questions well, but struggled when a process had edge cases or the content behind it was incomplete. The issue usually wasn’t model capability. It was that the page itself didn’t fully support a confident answer.


#### 2. We had to get much stricter about boundaries


In early iterations, DOT sometimes tried a little too hard to be helpful. That’s a common failure mode for AI systems. So we made the boundaries more explicit: when DOT should answer directly, when it should route someone to a human, and how to say “I can’t help with that yet” clearly and usefully.


#### 3. We had to tune for usefulness, not just correctness


We also learned that a technically correct answer can still be a poor support experience if it’s too long, too vague, or too formal. Tone and structure mattered more than we expected. We iterated on response style so DOT felt faster and more practical, not just accurate.


# How we evaluated the rollout


Before launch, we tested DOT against real support scenarios — the kinds of questions designers were already asking. We used evaluation to pressure-test response quality, routing logic, and whether the source material actually supported the answers we expected.


Then we looked at channel-level outcomes after launch. The goal wasn’t just to prove that DOT could answer a prompt in isolation. It was to understand whether the help experience itself was improving.


We analysed 176 threads in #help-design-ops across 18 months: 155 threads before DOT and 22 threads after launch. The post-launch sample is still relatively small, so we’re treating this as directional early data rather than a final verdict. Even so, the shift was clear.


Metric Before DOT After DOT Change


**Average first response time** 14.2 hours Seconds from DOT / 7 hours from humans 84% faster


**Questions with no reply** 33 of 153 threads = 21% Approximately 0% Eliminated


**Reply rate** 78.6% 100% +21 percentage points


**DOT handling rate** 0% Approximately 70% of threads New capacity


**Process questions reaching humans** 15 of 153 threads = 9.8% 0 of 22 threads = 0% Deflected


**ADS / design system questions reaching humans** 3 of 153 threads = 2% 0 of 22 threads = 0% Deflected


### **The strongest signal was also the simplest one: before DOT, roughly 1 in 5 questions went unanswered. After launch, that dropped to effectively zero.**


That’s the result we care about most. Faster answers are good. Consistent answers are good. But the biggest improvement was coverage. DOT helped close the gap on the questions that would otherwise have been missed entirely.


# What changed


DOT gave us more than a faster reply in Slack. It changed how the team thinks about operational knowledge.


- **Designers got answers faster.** For common tooling questions, the experience shifted from waiting hours to getting an answer in seconds.
- **Coverage improved.** The system became much better at catching routine requests that previously might have gone unanswered.
- **Humans got time back.** When repeatable questions are handled well by an agent, the team can spend more time on judgment-heavy, ambiguous, or strategic work.
- **Documentation quality went up.** The pressure of supporting an agent improved the clarity and usefulness of our Confluence content.
- **We now have a repeatable pattern.** The trigger → instructions → knowledge model gives us a practical way to extend DOT to new scenarios over time.


# What’s next


We launched DOT narrowly on purpose. Tooling support was the right place to start because it was high-volume, clearly bounded, and grounded in documentation we could improve. From here, the opportunity is to expand carefully into adjacent Design Ops scenarios where the same pattern applies.


That does not mean making DOT answer everything. It means being deliberate about where an AI teammate creates real value, where strong source material exists, and where the handoff to humans is clear.


We’re also continuing to build the governance side of the system: clearer ownership of knowledge pages, tighter maintenance rhythms, and a more durable way to keep the content trustworthy as policies, tools, and processes change.


# What other teams can take from this


You do not need to be an engineering team to build something useful with AI. But you do need a strong operational foundation.


The biggest takeaways from our experience are:


1. **Start with a real problem, not a vague ambition:** Narrow, high-frequency requests are the best place to begin.
2. **Treat documentation like product infrastructure:** If your knowledge is messy, your agent will be too.
3. **Design the behavior intentionally:** Voice, boundaries, and escalation paths are not cosmetic details. They are part of the quality system.
4. **Evaluate honestly:** Use real questions, watch where the agent fails, and let those failures tell you what to fix.
5. **Expand only when the foundation is ready:** A smaller, trustworthy agent beats a broader one that guesses.


For us, the real story isn’t that Design Ops built an AI teammate without writing code. It’s that building the agent forced us to strengthen the system around it: the content, the structure, the ownership, and the support model itself.


**That’s what made DOT useful. And that’s the part we think will matter for other teams too.**
